rv.q: The Royal Shakespeare Company's stellar stage show has all the thrillingly staged battles, gory deaths and, yes, dragons that the most bloodthirsty fan could hope for.
This prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance.
It’s a triumph; a soaring, surging spectacle and a latter-day history play, both serious and popular.

The script – by Every Brilliant Thing writer Duncan MacMillan – has a lot of heavy lifting to do to explain all this to those who may be rusty on their Westerosi history, and occasionally slips into clunky exposition, with characters stating their names, hopes, dreams and painful backstories as though in an introductory therapy session.
Inevitably, the first 40 minutes or so is largely concerned with exposition and introductions of Houses, characters and organisations.
From the moment you step into the auditorium, it’s clear that this is a spectacle unlike anything you’ve seen before.
The Mad King is a triumphant tragedy that perfectly captures the spirit of George R.R. Martin’s work and transposes it to a new medium.
Judging it on its own merits transforms The Mad King into a masterpiece of pure Shakespearean art, rather than a prequel to a once-great-now-middling fantasy TV series.
Thankfully, the Mad King largely succeeds on all fronts, the uninitiated bedazzled by a multitude of brilliantly staged battles, skirmishes and jousts, each handsomely choreographed.
It undoubtedly makes for an entertaining night out, and one I can’t imagine will not find its way to London, New York, and beyond.
The Game of Thrones franchise has yet another worthwhile and lucrative spin-off on its hands.
This is one of the RSC's most ambitious productions in recent years, and remarkably, it delivers.

cn.t: Critics praise this ambitious RSC production as a gripping, spectacular prequel that successfully resolves franchise mysteries with Shakespearean scope, stunning stagecraft, and propulsive energy that satisfies devoted fans.

ta: Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Waterside, Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire CV37 6BB
